design_detail: Described by its authors as a critical review; classified here as a systematic review without meta-analysis (as for sc_lappin_2017) because it reports its search (PsycINFO and Medline, July to September 2008, no date limits, 46 search terms pairing 'ecstasy' and 'MDMA' with the names of executive tasks and with 'visuospatial', 'word fluency' and 'verbal fluency'), explicit eligibility criteria and a structured extraction of all 33 included studies (Table 2). Synthesis is narrative and by counting studies, within four executive processes (updating, shifting, inhibition, access to long-term memory) and visuospatial memory; no appraisal of the included studies' risk of bias and no statistical synthesis. Many of the updating and visuospatial studies are the review authors' own.
can_establish: Which executive working memory tasks have and have not shown differences between people who use ecstasy, not intoxicated at testing, and comparison groups in the studies found up to 2008, and how those studies tried to control for other drug use.
cannot_establish: That ecstasy causes executive deficits (all but one included study were cross-sectional or quasi-experimental); the size of any deficit (no effect sizes were pooled); or that the pattern is free of selection and publication bias (no appraisal, English-language peer-reviewed studies only, many by the reviewers themselves).

sample.recruitment: Two databases searched July to September 2008 with no date limits (Method › Identification of Studies, p. 160); 59 studies found and screened against the criteria, 33 included (p. 161). Included studies were mostly from the UK, with others from Germany, the Netherlands, Spain, Hong Kong and the USA; samples community-recruited or predominantly student (Table 2, pp. 162-166).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: New empirical findings or attempted replications on a task empirically linked to an executive process (Table 1, p. 160) or on memory for the spatial location of single elements of a display; peer-reviewed journals; English; a stated minimum time since last ecstasy use, so that testing under the influence was excluded. Excluded: review articles, conference and thesis abstracts, and results reported only as composite measures (p. 161).
sample.demographics: Not applicable at review level. Group sizes in Table 2 range from about 10 to over 100; mean ages mostly early twenties.
sample.selection_effects: Two databases with task-specific terms, English only, no grey literature or reference-list searching reported, and who screened and extracted is not stated. Eight of the nine updating studies are by some combination of the review's authors (p. 161), and samples overlap between several of them (27 of the 44 people in one study were also in another, p. 161; 27 of 104 in a third, p. 170).

exposure.measurement: As reported by the primary studies (self-reported lifetime tablets or episodes); where none was reported, the reviewers recorded an implied estimate from the data available (Data Extraction, p. 161).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Mean lifetime use in Table 2 from about 20 exposures to more than 1,000 tablets; time since last use from about 1 day to more than 2 years (Table 2, pp. 162-166).
exposure.polysubstance: Recorded for each study as polydrug-using, cannabis-using, near-drug-naive or drug-naive comparison groups, together with the statistical controls used (ANCOVA, matched groups, exclusion of people exposed to a drug, correlations) (Data Extraction, p. 161; Table 2). Cannabis was present in every ecstasy group except in one Hong Kong study, and was relatively rare in one US study (p. 173).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Abstinent means not under the influence at testing, even if use was fairly recent (Introduction, p. 160); minimum intervals in the included studies ranged from about a day to months (Table 2).

comparison.controls: Varies by study: polydrug-using, cannabis-using, near-drug-naive or drug-naive comparison groups (Table 2).
comparison.matching: Recorded per study in Table 2 (group designs and covariates).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review states that cross-sectional designs make it impossible to rule out pre-existing differences as a cause of performance differences; only one included study was prospective (pp. 172-173).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Mostly yes (polydrug or cannabis-using comparison groups).

outcomes.instruments: Tasks listed in Table 1 (p. 160): updating (letter memory, spatial sequences, tone monitoring, computation span, reading span, consonant updating, operation span, keep track, random number generation), shifting (Wisconsin Card Sorting, plus/minus, number/letter, local/global), inhibition (random letter and number generation, Stroop, Tower of Hanoi or London, antisaccade, stop signal), access to long-term memory (Chicago word fluency, random letter generation; the FAS task added as a close variant), and spatial-location memory tasks.
outcomes.validity_norms: The mapping of tasks to executive processes is taken from latent-variable and factor-analytic studies (Miyake et al.; Fisk and Sharp) (p. 160).
outcomes.operationalization: A deficit is a statistically significant difference between groups on a dependent variable, as reported by the primary study; studies are counted as showing or not showing a deficit on each task.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates; the reviewers decided statistical analysis would not serve their aim of mapping deficits across executive processes (Results › Overview, p. 161). Figures given: the largest updating difference among 5 studies reporting span scores was 2.48 span items, 2.75 in people abstinent for at least 6 months vs 5.23 in polydrug controls (Wareing et al., 2005, as summarized, p. 161); computation span deficits were reported in 7 of 9 updating studies (p. 161); deficits in visuospatial tasks in 11 of 18 studies and none in 12 (some studies in both, Tables 3 and 4, pp. 170-171).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable at review level; the primary studies' covariates are recorded in Table 2.
analysis.selective_reporting: The review's own selection of tasks excludes studies of other executive tasks that reported deficits (p. 174). Several findings are discussed in terms of the authors' own studies. No list of the 26 excluded studies is given.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 33 mostly small cross-sectional studies, differences between people who use ecstasy and comparison groups were reported most often on computation span and consonant updating (mostly the reviewers' own studies) and on visuospatial tasks with higher processing demand; shifting tasks rarely showed differences; inhibition and access to long-term memory gave inconsistent results; and the links between deficits and amounts of ecstasy or other drugs were inconsistent.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Discussion say evidence of deficits was strongest for updating of verbal material and for demanding visuospatial tasks, that shifting appears relatively immune and that inhibition and access to long-term memory are unclear (pp. 159, 172), which matches the vote counts. The review calls the updating effects fairly robust (p. 167) while noting in the same summary that correlations with ecstasy and other drug use were inconsistent and that controlling for cannabis removed deficits on two other updating tasks (pp. 167-168). It does not flag that most of the updating evidence comes from its own authors' overlapping samples, and its conclusion that cross-sectional designs are a necessary means (p. 173) is not matched by any appraisal of their risk of bias.

timeline.event: Wareing and colleagues report impaired random letter generation in 10 people currently using and 10 who had stopped using ecstasy, with mean lifetime use above 1,000 tablets; two later studies by the same team did not replicate it (as summarized, pp. 169-170).
Halpern and colleagues' pilot in a region with low exposure to other drugs: a Wisconsin Card Sorting difference only for 11 people with heavier use (as summarized, p. 168).
Wareing and colleagues: computation span 2.75 vs 5.23 span items in people abstinent at least 6 months vs polydrug controls (as summarized, p. 161).
Prospective cohort of people starting ecstasy use: no visuospatial (line orientation) difference; the only genuinely prospective study among the 33 (pp. 166, 172).

A later systematic review restricted to at least 6 months of abstinence could not pool executive function and found mostly no significant differences between abstinent and MDMA-naive groups, with a trend in four studies by the same author (Ung et al., 2026, pp. 279-280).

replication.where_it_stands: A map of which executive tasks have shown differences, up to 2008. Its central updating result rests mainly on the reviewers' own overlapping samples and has not been tested by an independent pooled analysis in the papers read in this batch. The later review of sustained abstinence (Ung et al., 2026) did not pool executive function.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Edge Hill University, Liverpool John Moores University and the University of Central Lancashire (p. 159). The authors wrote eight of the nine updating studies and several of the visuospatial studies they review (p. 161; Table 2). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered systematic review with meta-analysis of the same executive tasks, with independent duplicate screening and risk-of-bias appraisal and with each sample counted once; and new studies of updating tasks by independent groups, with matched polydrug controls and testing before use.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people who use ecstasy, not intoxicated at testing), comparison groups, and outcomes (named executive tasks and spatial-location memory) are specified (pp. 159-161).
Cross-sectional and the one prospective study were included without an explanation of the choice of designs before the Discussion's argument that cross-sectional designs are necessary (p. 173).
Two databases with stated terms and dates, but English only and peer-reviewed only without justification, no reference-list, grey-literature or expert searching (pp. 160-161).
Extraction is described (p. 161), but not who did it or whether two people did.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: 59 studies screened and 33 included; the 26 excluded are not listed.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 2 gives for every study the country, sample source, group sizes and ages, time since last use, lifetime use, comparison groups' drug use, tasks, statistical controls and main findings (pp. 162-166).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No appraisal tool; control of other drug use and the testing of ANCOVA assumptions are discussed study by study, but selection bias and the other bias domains are not assessed.

domains.note: The Discussion considers the cross-sectional designs, residual confounding by cannabis and other drugs, and the limits of ANCOVA when interpreting the findings (pp. 172-173).
Inconsistent findings across tasks are discussed in terms of task demands, dependent variables, control of cannabis and time since last use (pp. 167-172).
No statistical synthesis; publication bias is not discussed.

domains.note: No funding or conflict-of-interest statement, although the authors review many of their own studies.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence because four critical items are not met: no protocol (item 2), a restricted search (item 4), no list of excluded studies (item 7) and no risk-of-bias appraisal (item 9); items 11, 12 and 15 do not apply. The review is transparent about its search, criteria and data (Table 2 is a usable catalogue) and its conclusions follow its vote counts, but the vote counts are not weighted by study quality or sample overlap, and much of the positive updating evidence is the reviewers' own. It may be cited for which tasks have and have not shown differences up to 2008 and for the only prospective study being the only one; it may not be cited for the size of any deficit or for a causal effect of ecstasy.

key_findings.finding: 33 studies were included from 59 found in PsycINFO and Medline (searched July to September 2008), all but one cross-sectional; inclusion required peer-reviewed English-language reports and a minimum time since last ecstasy use.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Conclusions (p. 159); Method › Identification of Studies, 1st paragraph (begins p. 160, continues p. 161) and 2nd paragraph (p. 161)

key_findings.finding: Updating: 9 studies, all but one by some combination of the review's authors; 7 reported computation span deficits; of 5 reporting span scores, the largest difference was 2.48 span items (2.75 in people abstinent for at least 6 months vs 5.23 in polydrug controls). Samples overlap: 27 of 44 people in one study were also in another.
key_findings.locator: Results › Ecstasy and Executive Updating, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Computation span deficits remained when cannabis, alcohol and nicotine (and in one study amphetamine and cocaine) were controlled by ANCOVA, and after excluding people exposed to amphetamine, cocaine or poppers; but correlations of performance with ecstasy and cannabis use were inconsistent across studies.
key_findings.locator: Results › Ecstasy and Executive Updating, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The reviewers call the updating effects on computation span and consonant updating fairly robust, noting deficits in people abstinent at least 6 months after more than 400 tablets on average; but correlations with use of ecstasy and other drugs were not consistent, and controlling for cannabis left no ecstasy-related deficit on two other updating tasks (reading span, keep track).
key_findings.locator: Results › Ecstasy and Executive Updating, 5th and 6th paragraphs (6th begins p. 167, continues p. 168)

key_findings.finding: Shifting: 6 studies; no differences on plus/minus or number/letter tasks or on the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test where other drug use was controlled by matched groups; in one study polydrug controls did worse than people using ecstasy; the only Wisconsin difference came from 11 people with heavier use in a region where cultural and religious norms limited exposure to other drugs. The reviewers find little evidence of impaired shifting.
key_findings.locator: Results › Ecstasy and Executive Shifting, 1st to 3rd and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Inhibition: 17 studies; standard Stroop measures showed no deficit in 6 of 8 Stroop studies and equivocal results in 2, including a Hong Kong study of 100 people who used ecstasy but no other illicit drugs, in which performance was not significantly worse after correction for multiple comparisons; an early random letter generation deficit (10 people currently using and 10 who had stopped) was not replicated. The reviewers find little evidence of impaired inhibition.
key_findings.locator: Results › Ecstasy and Executive Inhibition, 1st paragraph (begins p. 168, continues p. 169), 5th paragraph (pp. 169-170) and 6th paragraph (p. 170)

key_findings.finding: Access to long-term memory: the Chicago word fluency task showed deficits in 3 studies (overlapping samples); the FAS task showed deficits in 3 studies and none in 3; the reviewers call the results contradictory.
key_findings.locator: Results › Ecstasy and Access to LTM, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Visuospatial memory: 18 studies; 11 reported a deficit or a relation with ecstasy use on at least one measure (Table 3) and 12 reported none on some task (Table 4); deficits were reported in people abstinent at least 6 months in 2 studies and in groups with mean lifetime use of 149.69 and 169 tablets; the reviewers link deficits to tasks with higher executive demand.
key_findings.locator: Results › Ecstasy and Visuospatial Memory, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 170-171), 4th paragraph (p. 172); Tables 3 and 4 (p. 171)

key_findings.finding: Overall conclusion: deficits seem particularly evident in updating of verbal and visuospatial material and in visuospatial tasks with high executive demand; shifting appears relatively immune; evidence for inhibition and access to long-term memory is weak and ambiguous.

Only one included study was genuinely prospective (people tested before first ecstasy use); the others were cross-sectional or quasi-experimental, which makes it impossible to rule out pre-existing differences; the reviewers argue that prospective studies are slow and risk too little use by follow-up, and that experimental exposure would be unethical.

Cannabis was present in all ecstasy groups except in the Hong Kong study; ANCOVA removes variance shared between ecstasy and the covariate, so interactions cannot be studied, and its results are invalid without homogeneity of regression, which several studies did not report.
The reviewers note that laboratory tasks are proxies for everyday behaviour and that evidence of everyday cognitive problems in people who use ecstasy is self-reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion describes the prospective study of people starting ecstasy use as reporting mean use of 3.2 tablets after 3 years (p. 173); in that study follow-up took place within 3 years of baseline, a mean of 11.1 months later in the ecstasy group (Schilt et al., 2007, p. 731).
reporting_issues.consequence: Overstates the length of follow-up of the only prospective study.

reporting_issues.issue: Overlapping samples are noted for some updating and word-fluency studies (27 of 44; 27 of 104), but studies are still counted separately in the tallies of studies showing deficits.
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of independent samples behind the updating and word-fluency findings is smaller than the study counts suggest.
